extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public interested in manners, satire, and moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: Short, satirical essays offering moralizing and humorous prescriptions about social behaviour, clubs, love, beauty, and theatrical taste; mixes anecdote, mock-regulation, and moral precepts. Useful as a model for witty social satire and prescriptive comic commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission requirement for the Amorous Club
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mistress, and a Poem in her Praise, will introduce any Candidate: Without the latter no one can be admitted; for he that is not in love enough to rhime, is unqualified for our Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership requires both an object of affection (a named mistress) and a composed poem in her praise; the ability to rhyme is treated as proof of sufficient passion. (Example: 'A Mistress, and a Poem in her Praise, will introduce any Candidate.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Expulsion for speaking disrespectfully of women
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak disrespectfully of any Woman, is Expulsion from our gentle Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute rule: criticizing or speaking ill of any woman triggers removal from the club. This functions as both moral injunction and a comic rule of the club's constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial/behavioural performance norms (Amorous Club)
rubrics_metrics.description: We look upon a Man as no Company, that does not sigh five times in a Quarter of an Hour; and look upon a Member as very absurd, that is so much himself as to make a direct Answer to a Question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership implies performative conventions: exaggerated sighing, affectation, and avoiding straightforward answers are the expected signs of proper participation. These are comic behavioural standards used to satirize university affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidency bestowed by 'Dignity of Passion'
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Presidentship is bestow'd according to the Dignity of Passion; ... If any Man has declared the Violence of his Flame in more pathetick Terms, he is made President for that Night, out of respect to his superior Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership role is awarded on the basis of the most rhetorically or affectively demonstrative display of love; rhetorical intensity and pathetic expression are the selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club constitution features (secrecy, unlimited number, Druids-like statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Constitution runs counter to that of the Place wherein we live: ... our Number is unlimited; and our Statutes are like those of the Druids, recorded in our own Breasts only, and explained by the Majority of the Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal rules are comic and informal: secrecy, flexible membership, and internal majority interpretation are explicit structural features; useful as a satirical model of mock-institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Features alone do not make handsomeness
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Woman can be Handsome by the Force of Features alone, any more than she can be Witty only by the Help of Speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty (like wit) requires internal qualities, not mere physical features. Use this as a moral axiom in satire to argue for substance over surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Pride and affectation spoil beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: That Pride destroys all Symmetry and Grace, and Affectation is a more terrible Enemy to fine Faces than the Small-Pox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against pride and artificial behaviour; incomic moralizing, show how vanity and affectation negate natural grace—an anti-pattern for those seeking genuine charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Truthfulness (integrity) as a condition of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Woman is capable of being Beautiful, who is not incapable of being False.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is tied to moral integrity; falseness undermines true beauty. Although phrased negatively in the original, the intended rule is: capacity for truthfulness (incapacity for falsehood) is required for true beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: What is odious in a friend is deformity in a mistress
rubrics_metrics.description: That what would be Odious in a Friend, is Deformity in a Mistress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social tolerances differ by relationship: faults that might be excused in a friend are intolerable in a lover; use this to critique social expectations and double standards in comic moral essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art of assisting beauty (virtue over cosmetics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true Art of assisting Beauty consists in Embellishing the whole Person by the proper Ornaments of virtuous and commendable Qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive rule: improving appearance should focus on cultivating virtuous qualities (good humour, innocence, piety, truth) rather than mere cosmetic aids. Example: contrast between a picture's colours and the 'irradiating Power' of the mind in Milton's Eve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers' licence to use masks/personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Wits were privileged to wear what Masks they pleased in all Ages; and that a Vizard had been the constant Crown of their Labours...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defends the use of pseudonyms, fictional personae, or masks by writers and satirists; presented as a historic precedent and rhetorical device—useful as authorization for satirical voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of spectacle to subject (theatrical appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some at the Table urged that a Puppet-Show was not a suitable Entertainment for Alexander the Great; and that it might be introduced more properly, if we suppose the Conqueror touched upon that part of India which is said to be inhabited by the Pigmies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises (satirically) the criterion that theatrical devices and spectacles should suit the dignity and subject of the piece; the text also lampoons trivial objections and illustrates how comic taste debates can be frivolous.
